lessons.title: Chapters 1–3: The Door, the Will and Dr Jekyll

before.content_html:
Chapter 1: Story of the Door

The novella opens with Mr Utterson and his cousin Richard Enfield on their regular Sunday walk. They pass a mysterious, neglected door in an otherwise respectable street. Enfield tells Utterson a disturbing story: he once saw a small, ugly man trample over a young girl in the street “like some damned Juggernaut.”

The man was Mr Hyde. When confronted, Hyde showed no remorse but agreed to pay compensation. He disappeared through the mysterious door and returned with a cheque signed by Dr Jekyll. Enfield and Utterson agree never to speak of the matter again — a very Victorian response, prioritising discretion over truth.

Key Fact

The trampling of the girl is the reader’s first encounter with Hyde’s violence. Stevenson deliberately makes the victim a child to emphasise Hyde’s complete lack of moral boundaries.

Chapter 2: Search for Mr Hyde

Utterson goes home and reads Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde in the event of Jekyll’s death or “disappearance.” The word “disappearance” troubles Utterson deeply. He visits Dr Lanyon, an old friend of Jekyll’s, who dismisses Jekyll’s recent scientific work as “unscientific balderdash.”

Utterson begins to stake out the mysterious door. When he finally meets Hyde, he is struck by an overwhelming sense of repulsion. He describes Hyde as giving “an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation.” This is crucial — Hyde’s evil is felt rather than seen.

Throughout the novella, characters struggle to describe what is wrong with Hyde. Enfield says he is “not easy to describe” and gives “a strong feeling of deformity.” Utterson notes “deformity without any nameable malformation.” Stevenson deliberately makes Hyde’s appearance vague and unsettling. This mirrors the Victorian difficulty in confronting evil directly — they can sense it but cannot name it.

Chapter 3: Dr Jekyll Was Quite at Ease

Utterson visits Jekyll at one of his dinner parties. Jekyll is charming, sociable and entirely at ease — the complete opposite of Hyde. When Utterson raises concerns about the will, Jekyll becomes evasive and asks Utterson to drop the subject. He insists: “the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde.”

This chapter establishes the contrast between Jekyll and Hyde. Jekyll is warm, generous and respected; Hyde is cold, violent and repulsive. Yet Jekyll is clearly hiding something — his discomfort when Utterson mentions Hyde reveals the anxiety beneath his polished surface.

Key Fact

Jekyll’s claim that he “can be rid of Mr Hyde” at any time proves tragically wrong. This is an example of dramatic irony — the reader later discovers that Jekyll loses control of the transformations entirely.

Stevenson uses Utterson as the main narrative perspective for most of the novella. As a lawyer, Utterson is rational, restrained and trustworthy — making him a reliable guide for the reader. But his rationality also limits what we can know. He cannot understand Jekyll’s experiment because it is beyond rational explanation. The restricted perspective builds suspense and mirrors Victorian society’s refusal to look too closely at uncomfortable truths.

Stevenson’s Methods in Chapters 1–3

These opening chapters establish several key techniques that Stevenson uses throughout the novella:

Mystery and withholding: Stevenson reveals information slowly. The reader, like Utterson, must piece together clues. The connection between Jekyll and Hyde is not explained until the final two chapters.

Setting as symbolism: The mysterious door — blistered, neglected, with “no bell nor knocker” — represents the hidden side of Jekyll’s life. It is the back entrance to his laboratory, a passage between his respectable home and his secret world.

Fog and darkness: London is repeatedly described in terms of fog, shadows and gaslight. The fog symbolises the obscured truth and moral confusion at the heart of the story.

lessons.title: Chapters 7–10: The Last Night and Jekyll’s Statement

before.content_html:
Chapter 7: Incident at the Window

Utterson and Enfield pass Jekyll’s house and see him sitting at an upstairs window, looking “like some disconsolate prisoner.” They exchange pleasantries, and for a moment Jekyll seems to relax. Then, suddenly, a look of terror crosses his face, and he slams the window shut.

Utterson and Enfield walk away in silence, both deeply shaken. Stevenson never explains what happened at the window — the reader must infer that Jekyll was beginning to transform into Hyde involuntarily. This is the novella’s most chilling moment of withholding.

Key Fact

The window scene mirrors the opening “door” scene. Both involve Utterson and Enfield witnessing something disturbing connected to Jekyll’s house, and both end with a silent agreement not to discuss it. This structural echo reinforces the theme of Victorian repression.

Chapter 8: The Last Night

Jekyll’s butler Poole comes to Utterson in a state of panic. He believes his master has been murdered and replaced by someone hiding in the laboratory. Poole says the voice behind the locked door no longer sounds like Jekyll — it sounds like Hyde.

Utterson and Poole break down the door with an axe. Inside, they find Hyde’s body on the floor, dressed in Jekyll’s clothes, which are “far too large for him.” He has taken poison. Jekyll is nowhere to be found.

This chapter is the novella’s climax. Stevenson builds tension through Gothic elements: the screaming wind, the silent servants gathered in the hall, the sounds of pacing behind the locked door. The axe breaking down the door symbolises the violent exposure of Jekyll’s secret — the barriers he built between his public and private selves are literally smashed apart.

Finding Hyde in Jekyll’s oversized clothes provides the final physical clue. Hyde is smaller because he represents the part of Jekyll that was suppressed and undeveloped — his evil side had less “exercise” than his good side.

Chapter 9: Dr Lanyon’s Narrative

The narrative shifts from third-person to Lanyon’s own account, contained in his sealed letter. Lanyon describes receiving a desperate letter from Jekyll, asking him to collect chemicals from the laboratory and give them to a stranger who would arrive at midnight.

The stranger turns out to be Hyde. In front of Lanyon, Hyde drinks the potion and transforms back into Jekyll. Lanyon is so horrified that his health collapses — this is the “shock” he mentioned in Chapter 6.

Key Fact

The shift to Lanyon’s first-person narrative is structurally significant. It moves the reader from Utterson’s limited, rational perspective to the direct testimony of someone who witnessed the impossible. This makes the supernatural element feel more real and immediate.

Chapter 10: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case

The final chapter is Jekyll’s own confession. He explains that he had always felt a duality within himself — a respectable public self and a hidden, pleasure-seeking private self. His experiment was designed to separate these two natures.

At first, Jekyll enjoyed the freedom of being Hyde. As Hyde, he could indulge in “undignified” pleasures without risking his reputation. But over time, Hyde grew stronger and more violent, while Jekyll grew weaker. Eventually, the transformations began happening involuntarily — Jekyll would wake up as Hyde without having taken the potion.

“Man is not truly one, but truly two” — Jekyll’s central insight, challenging the Victorian belief that identity is fixed and unified.

“I was slowly losing hold of my original and better self, and becoming slowly incorporated with my second and worse” — shows that evil, once indulged, takes over.

“It was Hyde, after all, and Hyde alone, that was guilty” — Jekyll tries to distance himself from responsibility, but the reader recognises this as self-deception.

The novella uses three different narrators: the third-person account focused on Utterson (Chapters 1–8), Lanyon’s first-person letter (Chapter 9), and Jekyll’s first-person confession (Chapter 10). Each narrator sees more of the truth than the last. This layered structure mirrors the peeling away of Jekyll’s disguise — the deeper we go, the closer we get to the horrifying reality.

before.content_html:
Dr Henry Jekyll

Jekyll is a wealthy, respected doctor and scientist. He is “a large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty” who hosts dinner parties and donates to charity. He represents the ideal Victorian gentleman: moral, successful and generous.

But Jekyll harbours a secret. In his “full statement,” he confesses that he always felt a duality within himself. He describes “those provinces of good and ill which divide and compound man’s dual nature.” He was not a hypocrite in the usual sense — he genuinely wanted to be good. But the pressure of Victorian respectability meant he had to suppress his desires entirely, rather than finding a healthy balance.

Key Fact

Jekyll does not create Hyde to be evil. He creates Hyde to experience freedom — to indulge his “undignified” pleasures without risking his reputation. The tragedy is that separating good from evil makes both sides more extreme.

Jekyll’s story follows a classic tragic pattern. His hamartia (tragic flaw) is his belief that he can control the experiment. At first, he transforms voluntarily and enjoys the freedom. Then Hyde grows stronger. The transformations become involuntary. Finally, the potion stops working, and Jekyll is trapped as Hyde permanently. His suicide is the only escape.

Stevenson suggests that repression is the true cause of Jekyll’s downfall. If Victorian society had allowed Jekyll to express all sides of himself, he would never have needed the experiment.

Mr Edward Hyde

Hyde is Jekyll’s alter ego — the physical embodiment of everything Jekyll represses. He is described as small, pale, and giving an impression of deformity. Characters who encounter him feel instinctive disgust but cannot explain why.

Hyde’s appearance is deliberately vague. Stevenson uses words like “troglodytic,” “ape-like” and “hardly human” to suggest he is less evolved than a normal person. This connects to Victorian fears about degeneration — the idea that humanity could evolve backwards.

Key Fact

Hyde is smaller than Jekyll because, as Jekyll explains, his evil side had “less exercise” — it had been suppressed for years. This physical detail reinforces the idea that repression stunts part of the self rather than eliminating it.

Hyde’s violence escalates throughout the novella. He tramples a child (Chapter 1), murders Sir Danvers Carew with “ape-like fury” (Chapter 4), and becomes increasingly uncontrollable. Each act is more extreme than the last. Stevenson uses this escalation to show that evil, once released from restraint, does not stay moderate — it grows.

Crucially, Hyde feels no guilt. Jekyll describes him as “pure evil.” This distinguishes Hyde from Jekyll, who does feel remorse but uses the separation of identity to avoid taking full responsibility.

The Relationship Between Jekyll and Hyde

Jekyll and Hyde are not simply “good” and “evil.” Jekyll himself is not entirely good — he created Hyde out of selfish desire for freedom. And Hyde is not a separate person but a part of Jekyll that has always existed. The novella’s central argument is that everyone contains both good and evil, and that trying to deny this makes things worse.

Even in his final confession, Jekyll refers to Hyde in the third person: “He, I say — I cannot say I.” He tries to maintain the fiction that Hyde is a separate being. But this is self-deception. Jekyll created Hyde, enjoyed being Hyde, and is ultimately destroyed by Hyde. They are the same person.

Stevenson uses this self-deception to criticise Victorian society more broadly. Just as Jekyll refuses to acknowledge his darker self, Victorian society refused to acknowledge the poverty, vice and cruelty that existed beneath its respectable surface.

before.content_html:
Mr Gabriel John Utterson

Utterson is the novella’s main focaliser for Chapters 1–8. He is a lawyer: rational, loyal and deeply private. Stevenson introduces him as a man of “rugged countenance” who is “lean, long, dusty, dreary” but somehow still “lovable.”

Utterson embodies Victorian respectability. He suppresses his own desires — he enjoys the theatre but has not been to one in twenty years. He drinks gin to “mortify a taste for vintages” (punishing himself for enjoying good wine). He tolerates the failings of others without judging them, preferring to maintain social harmony.

Key Fact

Utterson is a mirror of Jekyll — both repress their desires, but Utterson does so without catastrophic consequences. He represents what Jekyll could have been if he had accepted his limitations rather than trying to transcend them.

Utterson functions as a detective figure. He stakes out Hyde, examines the will, questions Lanyon and eventually breaks down Jekyll’s door. But his Victorian propriety limits his effectiveness — he refuses to open Lanyon’s sealed letter, avoids prying into Jekyll’s private life, and consistently chooses discretion over truth.

This makes Utterson both sympathetic and frustrating. The reader can see clues that Utterson misses or deliberately ignores. Stevenson uses this gap between what the reader suspects and what Utterson knows to build dramatic irony.

Dr Hastie Lanyon

Lanyon is an old friend of Jekyll’s and a fellow doctor. He is described as “hearty, healthy, dapper” and full of confidence. He represents orthodox science — rational, empirical and cautious.

Lanyon dismisses Jekyll’s experiments as “unscientific balderdash.” This disagreement ended their friendship years before the novella begins. When Lanyon finally witnesses Hyde’s transformation into Jekyll, the shock destroys him — he dies within weeks.

Key Fact

Lanyon’s death shows the danger of confronting truths that a person is not prepared for. His rational worldview cannot accommodate what he has seen. Stevenson suggests that some knowledge is too terrible for the human mind to bear — a classic Gothic theme.

Lanyon represents the Victorian scientific establishment — cautious, evidence-based and respectable. Jekyll represents the maverick scientist who pushes beyond accepted boundaries. Their disagreement mirrors real Victorian debates about the limits of science, particularly after Darwin’s theory of evolution challenged religious certainties.

Stevenson does not clearly side with either. Lanyon’s caution is admirable but ultimately leads to ignorance. Jekyll’s ambition is intellectually bold but morally reckless. Both approaches fail.

Richard Enfield

Enfield is Utterson’s cousin and walking companion. He is described as a “well-known man about town” — sociable, worldly and less restrained than Utterson. It is Enfield who tells the story of Hyde trampling the girl in Chapter 1, setting the plot in motion.

Despite being more open than Utterson, Enfield shares the same commitment to discretion. After telling the trampling story, he immediately suggests: “let us make a bargain never to refer to this again.” This instinct to suppress uncomfortable knowledge is central to the novella’s critique of Victorian society.

Poole (Jekyll’s butler) represents the servant class. His loyalty to Jekyll drives the climactic break-in scene. His willingness to act when his master is in danger contrasts with Utterson’s cautious hesitation.

Mr Guest (Utterson’s clerk) notices the matching handwriting. His observational skill as a professional handwriting analyst advances the plot where Utterson’s propriety would not.

The maid who witnesses the Carew murder is one of very few female characters. Her emotional, swooning response contrasts with the male characters’ restraint, reflecting Victorian gender expectations.

before.content_html:
Theme 1: Duality

Duality is the novella’s central theme. Stevenson argues that every human being contains both good and evil, and that trying to separate them is both impossible and dangerous.

Jekyll’s experiment is an attempt to split his “dual nature” into two separate beings. He describes “those provinces of good and ill which divide and compound man’s dual nature.” But the experiment fails because good and evil are not separable — they are woven into the fabric of every person.

Key Fact

Duality operates at every level of the novella: character (Jekyll/Hyde), setting (respectable front/decayed laboratory), narrative (multiple perspectives), and even the title (“Strange Case” suggests something that defies rational explanation).

Jekyll’s house has a grand, respectable front entrance on a “square of ancient, handsome houses” and a neglected back door opening onto a “blind forehead of discoloured wall.” The two entrances represent Jekyll’s two identities. Hyde uses the back door — literally entering through the hidden, shameful side of Jekyll’s life.

London itself is presented as a city of contrasts: wealthy streets sit alongside impoverished Soho; fog obscures the boundaries between respectability and vice. Stevenson uses the motif of fog to suggest that moral clarity is impossible in a society built on concealment.

Theme 2: Repression

Repression drives the entire plot. Jekyll creates Hyde because Victorian society demands that he suppress every “undignified” impulse. Rather than allowing himself small, harmless pleasures, he must maintain a facade of total respectability.

Stevenson’s message is clear: repression does not eliminate desire — it intensifies it. Jekyll’s suppressed urges, when finally released as Hyde, take their most extreme and violent form. If Jekyll had been able to live a more balanced life, he would never have needed the experiment.

Repression is not unique to Jekyll. Utterson denies himself the theatre and good wine. Enfield makes a “bargain” never to speak of Hyde again. Even Poole suppresses his fear until breaking point. Every character in the novella practises some form of self-denial, reflecting a society where concealment is a way of life.

Key Fact

The novella is set in an almost entirely male world. There are no significant female characters. This intensifies the theme of repression — Victorian masculinity demanded emotional restraint, self-control and the suppression of vulnerability.

Theme 3: Science and Its Limits

Jekyll’s experiment is a scientific endeavour — he mixes chemicals to create the transformative potion. But the experiment crosses a moral boundary. Lanyon calls it “unscientific balderdash,” not because the chemistry is wrong, but because it violates the natural order.

Stevenson wrote during a period of intense scientific debate. Darwin’s theory of evolution had shaken religious certainties. New research into psychology was suggesting that the human mind was more complex — and darker — than previously believed. The novella asks: should science explore every corner of human nature, even if the discoveries are horrifying?

Like Victor Frankenstein in Mary Shelley’s novel, Jekyll is a scientist who oversteps moral boundaries and creates a monster he cannot control. Both texts belong to the Gothic tradition, which frequently uses science as a source of horror. The message in both texts is similar: scientific ambition without moral restraint leads to destruction.

How the Themes Connect

The three themes are deeply interlinked. Victorian repression creates the conditions for Jekyll’s experiment. His scientific ambition provides the means. And the result reveals the duality at the heart of human nature. Stevenson’s novella is ultimately a warning: a society that refuses to acknowledge the darker side of human nature will be destroyed by it.

before.content_html:
Language: Key Techniques

Stevenson’s language is precise and purposeful. Every word choice contributes to the novella’s atmosphere of mystery, horror and moral unease.

Hyde is consistently described using animalistic imagery. He moves with “ape-like fury,” is called “troglodytic” (cave-dwelling), and hisses “like a cornered snake.” This language links Hyde to degeneration theory — the Victorian fear that humans could reverse-evolve into primitive creatures. By making Hyde animal-like, Stevenson suggests that evil is not a moral failing but a biological reality lurking inside everyone.

Characters repeatedly struggle to describe Hyde. Enfield says he is “not easy to describe” and gives “a strong feeling of deformity.” Utterson notes “deformity without any nameable malformation.” This technique of describing something by saying it cannot be described is called apophasis. It makes Hyde more terrifying because the reader must imagine the horror for themselves.

This linguistic vagueness also reflects Victorian society’s inability to confront evil directly. The characters can sense that Hyde is wrong, but their respectable vocabulary has no words for what they are feeling.

Key Fact

Stevenson uses pathetic fallacy extensively. London’s fog, darkness and gaslight mirror the moral confusion and hidden evil at the heart of the story. The city itself becomes a character — concealing, distorting and threatening.

Structure: Three Narratives

The novella’s structure is one of its most distinctive features. It uses three different structural layers:

Chapters 1–8: Third-person narrative focused on Utterson. The reader shares his limited perspective, piecing together clues alongside him.

Chapter 9: Lanyon’s first-person letter. A shift to direct testimony from someone who witnessed the transformation.

Chapter 10: Jekyll’s first-person “full statement.” The final revelation, told by the man at the centre of the mystery.

Each narrative layer reveals more of the truth. Utterson sees the outside; Lanyon witnesses the transformation; Jekyll explains everything. This structure mirrors the peeling away of a disguise — the deeper we go, the closer we get to the horrifying reality beneath the respectable surface.

The use of epistolary elements (letters and written statements) is also significant. The truth can only be told in writing, after death. In Victorian society, some truths were literally unspeakable — they could only be committed to paper and sealed away.

Key Fact

The novella ends with Jekyll’s statement, not with Utterson’s reaction. The reader never learns what happens after Jekyll’s death. This open ending forces the reader to draw their own conclusions about the meaning of the story.

Narrative Perspective and Reliability

Stevenson carefully controls what the reader knows and when. Utterson is a reliable narrator in the sense that he reports honestly what he sees. But his perspective is limited — he cannot understand what is happening because it is beyond rational explanation.

Jekyll, by contrast, is an unreliable narrator. Even in his “full statement,” he distances himself from Hyde (“He, I say — I cannot say I”) and minimises his own responsibility. The reader must decide how much to trust Jekyll’s version of events.

Stevenson draws on several Gothic conventions:

The doppelgänger — Hyde is Jekyll’s dark double, a common Gothic motif representing the hidden self.

The mad scientist — Jekyll, like Frankenstein, conducts an experiment that creates a monster beyond his control.

The discovered manuscript — The truth is revealed through found documents (Lanyon’s letter, Jekyll’s statement), a technique used by Gothic writers to create a sense of authenticity.

Atmosphere of dread — Fog, darkness, locked doors and screaming winds create a persistent sense of menace.
